title: The Artist Who Turned Cleaning into Art—And Got Famous!
summary: Have you ever thought that cleaning your room could be art? Mierle Laderman Ukeles did! Back in 1969, she was a mom trying to be an artist, and she got frustrated. She wrote a manifesto—a big declaration—saying that all the boring, everyday jobs like washing dishes and changing diapers were actually a kind of art. She called it "maintenance art." Now, a new documentary called Maintenance Artist tells her story. It shows how she became the artist-in-residence at the New York City Department of Sanitation—yep, the garbage collectors! For 40 years, she worked with sanitation workers, shaking their hands and even turning a garbage truck into a ballet. The movie has funny moments, like when a famous art critic called her and asked, "Are you real, or did someone make you up?" Ukeles points out that her male art heroes, like Jackson Pollock, never had to stop painting to change diapers. She says if she were a man, she probably wouldn't make maintenance art. The film shows her taking 700 Polaroid photos of maintenance workers in a skyscraper—not just for art, but to prove she wasn't a spy! She wanted to celebrate the people who keep our world running but rarely get thanked. The documentary is playing in theaters now, and it might make you look at the person sweeping the street a little differently.
why_it_matters: Ukeles' art might make you think twice about the people who clean your school or collect your family's trash, and realize that caring for our world is a kind of art everyone can do.

background_read: In the 1960s, many artists wanted to expand the definition of art beyond paintings and sculptures. Mierle Laderman Ukeles, an artist and mother, wrote a famous manifesto in 1969 that declared daily chores like cleaning and childcare as 'maintenance art.' She later became the official artist for New York City's sanitation department (the agency that collects garbage), where she worked with garbage collectors for 40 years. The new film 'Maintenance Artist' shows how she honored workers who keep cities running, pointing out that male art stars like Jackson Pollock (a famous painter) never had to juggle diaper-changing with their work.
Article_Structure: WHO: Mierle Laderman Ukeles, an artist and mother.
WHAT: She invented 'maintenance art' and spent decades as the artist-in-residence with New York's sanitation workers, shaking their hands and turning garbage trucks into art.
WHERE: New York City; her documentary is now playing in theaters.
WHY: To celebrate the invisible workers who keep the world running and to challenge the art world's idea of what counts as important art.

perspectives.description: Sanitation workers feel seen and respected, and audiences learn that art can honor the invisible labor that keeps society functioning.
Some art critics originally dismissed her work as silly, and some people still believe cleaning isn't 'real' art, so her ideas remain controversial.
Ukeles challenges us to rethink what we value: do we celebrate only the flashy and new, or do we also appreciate the daily acts of maintenance that make everything possible?
